items.title: Claude Code Adds "Code Mode": Agents Now Write JavaScript to Call Their Own Tools
items.summary: In the week of November 15, Anthropic shipped Claude Code v2.1.323 with Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript programs to invoke its tools instead of issuing one tool call at a time. It is off by default and can be disabled organization-wide. The same release wave also hardened the agent: v2.1.321 closed four permission and sandbox gaps — including a cp/mv-into-directory route that bypassed deny rules and an MCP OAuth redirect that could leak refresh tokens to another host — while v2.1.325 patched a security issue in zstd-compressed response decoding. Plugins can now declare engines["claude-code"] version ranges, and TypeScript hooks are type-checked at validation time.
items.impact: Code Mode is a genuine interface shift: rather than treating tools as fixed buttons, the agent programs them, enabling tighter loops and complex tool compositions. Combined with the permission fixes, it shows the friction moving from 'what the agent can do' to 'how safely it can do it' — the central engineering problem for autonomous coding agents.

items.title: Codex Tightens Trust: --sandbox No Longer Loads MCP Servers in Untrusted Folders
items.summary: OpenAI's Codex CLI reached v0.169.0 this week with a behavioural change that matters for CI. codex exec now keeps project configuration and MCP servers disabled in untrusted directories even with --sandbox workspace-write; teams must pass --trust explicitly to load them. The opt-in terminal workspace gained multiple side-chat tabs that survive a restart, and a Ctrl+S diagnostic ZIP export for locked-down environments. Across four releases, incremental tool updates became the default on Google Cloud Vertex AI, and features.multi_agent was deprecated in favour of agents.enabled.
items.impact: This is a supply-chain guardrail for agentic CI: a writeable sandbox is no longer treated as permission to auto-load a repo's MCP servers. Anyone running codex exec in automation should audit their trust flags now — the change silently breaks builds that relied on implicit project config.

items.title: "Thinking in Code": Agents Compress Their Own Output by 99.4%
items.summary: Context Mode, an emerging agent framework, shipped 15 releases in November built around a technique it calls Thinking in Code — agents emit compact scripts that compress their own tool output by roughly 99.4%, sharply cutting context-window consumption. It is part of a broader November pattern: Claude Code's Code Mode, Codex's programmable workspace, and a wave of context-compression tooling all converge on the same idea that code is the most token-efficient interface between a model and its tools.
items.impact: Context length and cost are the binding constraints on long-running coding agents. If agents can programmatically summarise and transform their own outputs, multi-hour autonomous sessions become far more economical — a lever that matters much more than marginal benchmark gains for anyone deploying agents at scale.

items.title: Huawei Cloud Launches CloudRobo-WM1.2, Its First Ascend-Native Embodied World Model
items.summary: On November 16 from 14:00 to 15:30 Beijing time, Huawei Cloud is holding an online launch for CloudRobo-WM1.2, the first Ascend-native embodied world model and the first native world model under its 'Industry AI Dream Factory' programme. A world model acts as an internal simulation of physical rules, letting a robot predict consequences and plan in unfamiliar settings before acting. The company says the model targets the hard bottlenecks in embodied AI — multimodal physical understanding, coupling world knowledge to action generation, scaling heterogeneous data, cross-embodiment generalisation and real-time inference cost. Partners including YiJiaHe, Topstar, iSoftStone and Galaxea are expected to sign on; Huawei has said it will not build robot bodies itself.
items.impact: This is China's AI infrastructure stack extending from text and images into physical-world reasoning, with domestic compute (Ascend) at the core. It reframes embodied AI competition from robot hardware toward a full 'model + compute + toolchain + scenario' system that other vendors can call into — a platform play worth watching closely.

items.title: Swiss Startup Unveils AIR: a Tendon-Driven Humanoid That Learns Factory Tasks on the Job
items.summary: At Humanoid Europe 2026 on November 15, Swiss company Embodied AI unveiled AIR, a humanoid designed to work beside people on factory floors rather than behind cages. Its arms are light and tendon-driven, with motors moved into the torso so they yield on contact, and it runs on wheels for stability on flat floors — safety by mechanical design, targeting ISO/TS 15066 with CE marking planned for 2027. AIR starts each job under human teleoperation, records every run, and its AI stack learns from those demonstrations until it can perform the task alone, typically within a month; what one robot learns transfers to the next. The company says it went from research to an industrial humanoid in nine months and hit 98% reliability on a cable-handling task against a 90% target.
items.impact: AIR attacks the real deployment gap — high-dexterity, frequently changing manual work — with a pragmatic mix of imitation learning, built-in safety and human fallback rather than promising full autonomy. Its 'learn from one shift, deploy in a month' model is a concrete template for how physical AI could actually enter factories at scale.
